prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "NEXTERA ENERGY INC" (ticker NEE), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "NEE", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: NextEra Energy, Inc.
result.industry: Electric utility and renewable power generation
markets: Regulated electricity supply in Florida (Florida Power & Light)
Wholesale renewable power: wind, solar and battery storage under long-term contracts (NextEra Energy Resources)
Power supply for large loads such as data centers

mission.plain: Provide reliable, affordable and increasingly clean electricity to homes and businesses while building the power infrastructure America needs.

about.plain: NextEra Energy owns Florida Power & Light, the company that sends electricity to about 12 million people in Florida. It also owns NextEra Energy Resources, which builds huge wind farms, solar farms and giant batteries across the US and sells the power to other utilities and big companies. It makes money by charging for the electricity it delivers and by selling power under long contracts. It is now also building power for data centers and plans to merge with Dominion Energy.
about.customers: Florida homes and businesses, plus utilities, power cooperatives and big tech companies like Google and Meta that sign long contracts to buy its power.
about.everyday: If you turn on a light or air conditioner in much of Florida, the electricity most likely comes from FPL, NextEra's utility.

money.plain: electricity for more than 6 million Florida customer accounts
wind, solar, battery and nuclear power sold under long contracts

money.part: Power for data centers and large loads
money.plain: multi-gigawatt power deals and campuses with Google, Meta and others
restarting a 615 MW Iowa nuclear plant with Google as main buyer
would add Virginia and Carolinas utilities, about $16.5B of yearly sales

result.summary: Yes. NextEra combines the largest US electric utility (FPL), which is a regulated local monopoly with an authorized 10.95% return on equity, with one of the largest US developers of wind, solar and battery storage, whose scale in buying equipment, financing and connecting projects lets it win contracts mainly on price. The weak spots are heavy debt, dependence on regulators and tax-credit policy, and a stock that trades like a bond when interest rates rise.

pricingPower.evidence: FPL's prices are set by the Florida PSC, which in January 2026 approved base revenue increases of $945 million (2026) and $705 million (2027) at a 10.95% allowed ROE; customers have little alternative so volumes hold, but increases need regulatory approval and face challenges (the Office of Public Counsel sought reconsideration in February 2026), while NEER 'primarily competes on the basis of price' for contracts.

moats.evidence: Its real intangible assets are its Florida service territory franchise and its reputation as a best-in-class renewable developer (Morningstar's Andy Bischof called it 'top-notch, best-in-class'); the consumer brand matters little.
FPL customers cannot easily switch to another wires utility, and NEER's 35,627 MW of contracted capacity is locked into long-term power purchase agreements.
Electricity supply does not get more valuable to each user as more customers join.

With about 80 GW of generation and storage capacity and roughly $24.6B of capital spending in 2025, NextEra buys turbines, panels and batteries and raises capital at a scale few rivals match, which lets NEER win contracts on price.
FPL is the regulated monopoly supplier for most of Florida's peninsula, a market where a second grid would make no economic sense.
It moved early into utility-scale wind and solar while fossil-heavy utilities hesitated, but peers have since copied the strategy.
Decades of experience in siting, permitting, interconnecting and financing renewable projects let it add backlog steadily (3.6 GW added in Q2 2026, backlog about 35.1 GW).
It holds a large pipeline of sites and grid interconnection positions plus nuclear units such as Seabrook, Point Beach and the Duane Arnold restart, assets that are hard to replicate.

customers.evidence: FPL keeps nearly all customers because it is the local monopoly, and big buyers return for more: Meta signed for 2.5 GW across 13 projects in December 2025 on top of about 500 MW already operating, and Google has about 3.5 GW in operation or under contract; residential satisfaction data were not checked.

talent.evidence: About 17,400 employees at end-2025; it is seen as a strong operator and long-tenured management (CEO John Ketchum joined in 2002), but no verified employer-ranking data were found.

product.evidence: Electricity is a commodity, but NextEra is the largest US electric utility and a leading developer of wind, solar and battery storage (about 22,404 MW wind, 10,504 MW solar and 5,177 MW batteries at NEER), which makes it a go-to supplier for hyperscalers.

competitors.name: Duke Energy Corporation
competitors.note: Neighboring regulated utility including Duke Energy Florida; competes for capital, data-center load and renewable buildout in the Southeast.

competitors.name: The Southern Company
competitors.note: Large Southeast regulated utility competing for data-center and industrial load and utility investment.

competitors.name: Dominion Energy, Inc.
competitors.note: Virginia/Carolinas utility serving the largest US data-center market; being acquired by NextEra (agreement dated May 15, 2026).

competitors.name: Constellation Energy Corporation
competitors.note: Largest US nuclear fleet; competes to sell clean power to hyperscalers and in wholesale markets.

competitors.name: Vistra Corp.
competitors.note: Competitive generator (gas, nuclear, solar, batteries) competing in wholesale and data-center power.

competitors.name: The AES Corporation
competitors.note: Renewables and storage developer signing long-term contracts with tech companies.

competitors.name: Brookfield Renewable Partners
competitors.note: Global renewables owner and developer; signs large clean-power deals with Microsoft and Google.

competitors.name: Invenergy
competitors.note: Large private US wind, solar and storage developer competing for PPAs and interconnection.

competitors.name: Iberdrola (Avangrid)
competitors.note: Spanish utility whose US arm Avangrid develops onshore wind and solar.

competitors.name: Orsted A/S
competitors.note: Global renewable developer with US onshore and offshore wind and solar.

competitors.name: American Electric Power Company
competitors.note: Large regulated utility and transmission owner competing for data-center load and capital.

competitors.name: Clearway Energy, Inc.
competitors.note: Contracted renewables owner competing for PPAs.

competitors.name: Engie SA
competitors.note: Major developer of US renewables and storage for corporate buyers.

threats: Rising interest rates: debt of about $110B at June 30, 2026 and interest expense that doubled to $4,572M in 2025 make it highly rate-sensitive.
Federal policy changes to renewable tax credits, tariffs on solar panels and batteries, or permitting could slow NEER's buildout.
Florida regulators and consumer advocates resisting rate increases (the 2025 rate agreement faced a reconsideration motion in February 2026).
Execution and regulatory risk in the roughly $65B all-stock Dominion Energy acquisition, needing approval from Virginia, North Carolina, South Carolina, FERC and the NRC.
Hurricanes hitting FPL's Florida service territory.
Competition from Constellation, Vistra, Brookfield and others for hyperscaler power contracts, and a shift toward gas and nuclear that is less proven for NextEra.
Deeply negative free cash flow (about -$12.1B in 2025) requiring continued debt and equity issuance.

ceo.name: John W. Ketchum
ceo.background: Lawyer and finance executive (JD and LLM in taxation, University of Missouri-Kansas City; BA economics and finance, University of Arizona); joined NextEra in 2002, former CFO and CEO of NextEra Energy Resources

c1.evidence: NextEra is a leader of US renewables and battery storage (about 5,177 MW of NEER batteries, 35.1 GW backlog), a fast-growing field, but its core is a century-old regulated utility rather than an emerging industry.

c2.evidence: Customers choose NEER mainly on price, which its scale supports, and Florida customers have no real alternative to FPL; the scale advantage is durable but rivals like Brookfield and AES compete closely.

c3.evidence: FPL is a household name in Florida and NextEra is the largest US electric utility, but most Americans outside Florida would not recognize the NextEra name.

c4.evidence: Management emphasises building America's energy infrastructure and clean power, but communications focus heavily on 8%+ adjusted EPS growth and dividend targets rather than a stated mission.

c6.evidence: “big utility, renewables leader, Florida Power & Light” — impressions are mostly positive among investors, but Florida consumers often complain about rate increases and the stock is seen as rate-sensitive.

c7.evidence: US electricity demand is rising with data centers and electrification; FPL alone reports about 21 GW of large-load interest, and NEER keeps adding gigawatts of backlog.

c8.evidence: It is expanding from renewables into gas, nuclear restarts (Duane Arnold), transmission, data-center campuses with Google and Meta, and the pending Dominion merger into Virginia and the Carolinas.

m1.evidence: Ketchum has laid out a clear plan to meet surging US power demand with renewables, storage, gas and nuclear, but it is an extension of NextEra's existing strategy rather than a new vision.

m2.evidence: Not a founder; a 24-year company veteran who sets long-dated targets (EPS growth through 2035) and is making a bold bet with the Dominion merger.

m4.evidence: No specific public evidence found on a servant-leadership style.

m5.evidence: NextEra's culture is known for execution and cost discipline in project development, and it is now co-developing digital operating platforms with Google, but it is not a product-invention culture.

m6.evidence: Ketchum is a tax lawyer and finance executive (former CFO), not an engineer.

m7.evidence: No controversies found, but there is little public evidence either way about his personal character beyond his business role.

m7b.evidence: No record found of Ketchum giving a commencement address at a top university.

m8b.evidence: Ketchum keeps a low, businesslike public profile.

m9.evidence: Adjusted EPS has met guidance ($3.71 in 2025, 2026 guidance $3.92–$4.02) and backlog has grown, but the stock at $79.80 (October 16, 2026) is about 19% below its May 1, 2026 high of $98.75.

m10.evidence: NextEra is known for low operating costs at FPL, but no well-known frugality symbols.

c10.evidence: It supplies power to about 12 million Floridians and clean power across 44 states, important but largely limited to the US.

p2.evidence: Building and running about 80 GW of power plants, nuclear units and a grid through hurricanes is very hard and essential to the economy.

f1.evidence: Operating revenues fell in 2021 ($17,069M from $17,997M) and 2024 ($24,753M from $28,114M) before rising to $27,412M in 2025.

f2.evidence: Operating margin was 28.4% in 2020, fell to 17.1% in 2021, then rose to 30.2% in 2025; margins swing with hedging gains and losses.

f3.evidence: Total debt was about $110.2B against only $2.9B of cash at June 30, 2026, though shareholders' equity was positive at $68.1B.

f4.evidence: Operating income rose from $5,116M (2020) to $8,280M (2025) and operating cash flow from $7,983M to $12,485M, but neither rose every year (cash flow dipped from $13,260M in 2024).

v1.evidence: FPL is often cited for low rates and reliability and NEER for low-cost renewables, but electricity is a commodity and customers often cannot choose.

v2.evidence: No verified employer ranking found for NextEra.

c5.evidence: If NextEra vanished, about 12 million Floridians would lose their electricity supplier and companies like Google and Meta would lose gigawatts of contracted clean power.
